articles.title: Australian politics live: Lambie compares ‘dangerous’ Hanson to Trump; NSW One Nation leader wants abortion ‘stopped’
articles.excerpt:
Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jacqui Lambie has warned Australians not to support a “dangerous” and “delusional” Pauline Hanson, drawing comparisons between the One Nati...
articles.body_text:
Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jacqui Lambie has warned Australians not to support a “dangerous” and “delusional” Pauline Hanson, drawing comparisons between the One Nation leader and controversial international leaders.

In a speech during adjournment last night in the Senate, the Tasmanian senator said she had received a stream of abuse after her impassioned defence of Andrew Hastie after he was repeatedly labelled a “traitor” in One Nation’s cartoon series.

double quotation markOne Nation whips up the anger and they tell people who to blame. That’s the populist trick … It’s a trick Australia, and we’ve got to wake up to it. Because every time a populist leader, like Trump or Farage, get any power, the lives of working people don’t get better. They get worse.

The outspoken senator criticised Donald Trump’s potential forever war with Iran while singling out Hanson’s support of his actions.

double quotation markYou’d put [Australian soldiers] back in another American forever war? [Hanson] is not only dangerous, she’s delusional!

Lambie said figures such as Trump and Nigel Farage were great at telling people they would fight for them while doing the opposite.

double quotation markSenator Hanson will be fine in her retirement, as will Nigel and Donald in theirs, because once again they are feathering their own nests … Australia can choose not to follow the ugly politics of populism, we can do better because we bloody are better.

And it’s not about right or left, it’s about respect and finding solutions, and not operating from a place of fear – whatever side you’re on.

Andrew Hastie says the national tone has “taken a real dip” with One Nation making politics personal and “Maga-style”.

It’s certainly personal for Hastie with One Nation targeting his Western Australian seat of Canning, and Hastie and Pauline Hanson currently feuding over a cartoon video that labelled the former SAS captain a “traitor”.

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Hastie says he hasn’t spoken to Hanson in the last week.

double quotation markThe national tone has take a real dip of late and become quite personal, US-style Maga politics have been run by One Nation, and I have decided to push back. We want to win the next election as the Coalition and it’s a three-cornered contest and the Liberal party should be striving to be number one on the ballot. That’s what I’ve been arguing for.

It seems like a pretty clear message to his party to push back hard on Hanson and One Nation.

Asked more explicitly if he’d be comfortable with the Coalition joining with One Nation to form government, Hastie says the Liberals need to focus on themselves … at least for now.

double quotation markOur primary vote is still very low compared to what it’s been in historic terms, we have to focus on being number one in terms of primary votes. Whatever happens after the election I don’t know. We’re fighting for our survival and we should be focused on that.

Sports precinct funding report reveals a ‘pattern of behaviour’, Wilson says

Tim Wilson says there are plenty of questions for Labor to answer over a report in the ABC which says health minister Mark Butler’s office asked an Adelaide council to put forward a $6m sports precinct upgrade for federal funding before any detailed costings or formal planning had been done.

Labor then awarded the project $5m of funding in the 2025 election – under the invite-only grant scheme.

Wilson tells News24 the government needs to explain who reached out to the council, who made the initial contact, what proposals were put forward and whether Butler is an honorary member of the club.

double quotation markI think what we’re now seeing is a pattern of behaviour. The prime minister gave a grant to a golf course in his electorate just around the corner from his home, of which he was a member, which he failed to declare. Now we have the health minister, the next wannabe prime minister, doing exactly the same thing.

I think the problem we’ve got is the government was in a desperate attempt before the last election to stay in office. Now, the election turned out differently than as it appeared in, say, November 2024. And so they scurry to try and dole out public money to get themselves in a winnable position. The problem is it’s now catching up with them.

‘Ball was dropped’ on antisemitism, former spy boss says

Former Asio boss Dennis Richardson told the Lowy Institute last night that the “ball was dropped” on antisemitism, but this morning says he won’t focus on any particular people to ascribe responsibility.

Speaking to RN Breakfast, Richardson says some things that were said in the public sphere, citing comments posted to social media by an Islamic preacher in November 2023, were not immediately and widely condemned as they should have been.

He adds the country needs to have a discussion about Islamic extremism without making Muslim Australians feel targeted.

double quotation markThat’s a difficult thing to do. However, I think one way to do it is to ensure that Muslim leaders are at the centre of any such discussion and guide that discussion in a way that Australian Muslims as a whole do not feel targeted. Because there is a real risk when you have a discussion about extremist Islam, you have a real risk that Muslims as a whole feel under pressure. Equally, if you don’t have that discussion, you play into the hands of extremists at the other end of the spectrum.

Asked whether the royal commission – which he was initially engaged in but then left – has heard from the right people and was doing the right work, he says everyone should withhold judgment until the final report is released later this year, but that it has already done an “outstanding” job of spotlighting the experiences of Jewish Australians.

Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you, thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started.

One Nation will continue dominating chatter across the halls of parliament today, and if you haven’t already, take a read of my colleague Sarah Martin’s piece on Pauline Hanson’s daughter working remotely without ministerial approval.

And what to do with AI and whether it will lead to the end of human civilisation? The issue has drastically ramped up in Canberra this week after a slow down warning from tech leaders, while creatives push for the government to hold strong on copyright protections.

It’s going to be another busy one – let’s get cracking.

Betting company Dabble has been fined more than $1m for continuing to send more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority also found the gambling company failed to close the betting accounts of 157 people who registered with Betstop, which helps people break their gambling addictions.

In a statement, Acma said Dabble sent more than 2,000 push notifications to 45 customers without including any information about the Betstop service, which is a legal requirement.

The watchdog has fined the company $1,069,200. According to Acma, Dabble has also been given a court-enforceable undertaking to guarantee future compliance with the rules.

Acma member, Carolyn Lidgerwood, said the breaches were serious and undermined the federal government’s harm minimisation strategy.

double quotation markPeople who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering. Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions.

BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules. The Acma will take action where wagering providers fail to meet their obligations.

NSW government to smooth transfer of rental bond from one property to the next from today

Renters in NSW will be able to transfer their bond from one property to the next from today, meaning they won’t need to come up with thousands of dollars upfront every time they move.

It’s expected Smart Rental Bonds will save more than two million renters across the state up to $4,000 each time they move home – though the online scheme costs $25 to use.

The NSW government will pay the landlord the bond upon the end of the lease, while the renter will repay the government.

Renters will need to pay the difference if the second bond is higher – equally they will be refunded the difference if it is cheaper, provided there is no agreed claim on the bond.

The NSW government scheme has already seen $1m in bond transfers in Penrith, Parramatta and the Central Coast, where it was rolled out early.

It follows similar moves to make renting fairer in NSW, including a ban on no grounds evictions, a limit of one rent increase a year, enforcing fee-free ways to pay rent and making it easier for people to have pets.

The head of One Nation in New South Wales has fronted a rally opposing “abortion up to birth” ahead of an expected vote in the upper house on Libertarian member John Ruddick’s bill to ban “sex-selective abortions” during private member’s business today.

Mike Newman appeared alongside members of fringe parties outside the state’s parliament house on Tuesday evening, where he claimed One Nation wanted to “stop” abortion rights. Stumbling upon his words, he told the crowd:

double quotation markWe want to stop it. We want to make sure that same-sex, sorry, abortion is stopped. We want to make sure that people have the right to life, and we will vote for you in favour of that.

Debate on Ruddick’s bill was adjourned in the June sitting week, and is expected to be decided via a conscience vote. Labor and opposition sources said the vote was expected to be close, or for support for Ruddick’s bill to fall slightly short.

The event follows another anti-abortion rally in June, attended by One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, where he piled pressure on Nationals MPs to vote on favour of the bill.

Some members were expected to be absent for today’s vote, including Shooters, Farmers and Fishers MLC Robert Borsak, who spoke in favour of the bill in June. A senior Liberal source said that without members including Borsak, there did not appear to be “any room or margin” which could deliver Ruddick’s bill.

UK ‘on track’ to begin building Aukus submarines, Marles says

Richard Marles was also asked about Aukus, and whether he was concerned about reports from the UK which indicated the Labour government was delaying its decision about beginning to build the boats by two years to 2028.

He said there was “no change” on Australia’s end in terms of the UK’s position and rejected that they were “red flags”.

double quotation markThe ultimate number of submarines is not the key issue here, the key issue is the development of the design, the pace of that which is happening.

The UK is on track to cut steel in respect of its first SSN Aukus submarine next year. It’s on track to have that submarine come off the production line in the UK in the late 2030s. That’s perfect timing in respect of what we’re doing … We are really comfortable with what is happening there.

Marles takes ‘comfort’ from AI company boss’s call for safeguards around the technology

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, says he is “comforted” by a recent essay from the boss of artificial intelligence company Anthropic which warned his industry must slow the pace in developing AI systems.

Appearing on ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening, Marles was asked about Dario Amodei’s comments urging governments to press pause on the AI revolution.

double quotation markI actually take comfort in Dario Amodei’s essay and the call he’s made … It’s firstly not about … stopping this all together but rather making sure that the development of the safeguards that are in place in respect of this technology is in front of the technological capability itself …

The technology is being developed very quickly, and … from an Australian point of view, our focus is making sure that, in seeing this as a revolutionary technology which can be doing so much good in Australia, that we do have in place … AI safeguards in Australia which make sure that this is a technology which will benefit Australians and not the other way around.

And it’s not about right or left, it’s about respect and finding solutions, and not operating from a place of fear – whatever side you’re on.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

Jacqui Lambie has launched a fiery attack on Pauline Hanson, urging Australians not to support the “dangerous” and “delusional” One Nation leader. More coming up.

articles.title: TRACE GALLAGHER: Common sense is alive in America. We just need to listen
articles.excerpt:
Anchor of "Fox News @ Night" Trace Gallagher joins Fox Across America With Jimmy Failla to talk about his new book, 'TURNS OUT THEY WERE RIGHT ALL ALONG: Lessons I Learned...Eventually'.

During the f...
articles.body_text:
Anchor of "Fox News @ Night" Trace Gallagher joins Fox Across America With Jimmy Failla to talk about his new book, 'TURNS OUT THEY WERE RIGHT ALL ALONG: Lessons I Learned...Eventually'.

During the first-ever Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas last week, there was a lot of talk about the "common sense revolution." It was familiar territory to me because every night on my evening newscast, "Fox News @ Night," we join the common sense revolution — you could say we started the common sense revolution more than four years ago. We like to call it "The Fox News @ Night Common Sense Department."

Common sense gives us a chance to take a deeper and sometimes snarkier take on one of the day’s big topics. The goal of the Common Sense Department is not to accuse Americans of not having common sense, but to remind Americans that we share a great deal of common sense. And when somebody or some group steps outside the boundaries of what we consider societal norms, we love to point out exactly why those boundaries exist. Those boundaries were built over many generations by people whose moral code was instilled through faith, family, friends and fortitude.

Trace Gallagher hosts "Fox News@Night" on Fox News Channel.

When I wrote my new book, "Turns Out They Were Right All Along," I first thought of naming the book "A Trace of Common Sense," a play on my name and the name of my segment. I soon realized that my stories are about more than common sense; my stories are about wisdom that has been gifted, sometimes forced upon me, by a group of amazing people. Some famous, some not, but all of them taught me that hard work and skill are important, while teamwork and luck are also extremely relevant. That means that, at some point, everyone needs to ride on the shoulders of giants — whatever shape or size those giants happen to come in.

Chief Breaking News Correspondent and Anchor Trace Gallagher's new book, "Turns Out They Were Right All Along,"  was published on Sept. 15 by HarperCollinsPublishers. (HarperCollins)

The reason the subtitle of my book is "Life Lessons I Learned Eventually" is because it often takes me a while to recognize solid advice. I have a tendency to wave off wisdom, thinking that I’m better off doing it my way. The problem is, my way is often the wrong way, which on second blush has reminded me to accept good wisdom at face value.

So, after spending years ignoring wisdom before finally accepting it, I now spend a great deal of time passing it on — not only in my book but also by mentoring young people, including young television news correspondents. I labor to convince these young people that America is filled with common sense as long as we are occasionally willing to listen to great wisdom, accept great wisdom and use great wisdom to achieve greatness.

Trace Gallagher serves as FOX News Channel’s (FNC) chief breaking news correspondent and was recently named anchor of FOX News @ Night (weeknights 12-1 AM/ET). Gallagher will take over the nightly newscast on October 3rd, anchoring from FNC’s Los Angeles bureau where he is based. Click here for more information on Trace Gallagher.

articles.title: US Senate crypto bill collapses in blow to industry
articles.excerpt: The United States Senate has failed to advance comprehensive cryptocurrency legislation backed by President Donald Trump in a major blow for digital-asset companies and Republicans who had championed ...
articles.body_text:
The United States Senate has failed to advance comprehensive cryptocurrency legislation backed by President Donald Trump in a major blow for digital-asset companies and Republicans who had championed the bill for months.

The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act failed on Tuesday to secure the 60 votes needed to advance to a debate in the Senate, with safeguards governing Trump’s extensive crypto interests among the biggest obstacles to a deal.

Four Republican senators – Jerry Moran, Rand Paul, Josh Hawley and Thom Tillis – joined all the Democrats in voting against it. The vote was 50-49 in favour.

The vote effectively put the bill on ice, as Congress is set to depart Washington this month ahead of the November midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of the House of Representatives and Senate.

Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said the bill posed “massive risks to families, our national security, and our economy”.

“And if that’s not bad enough, while Americans across the country suffer from an affordability crisis, this bill will turbocharge President Donald Trump’s ability to rake in billions and billions of dollars from crypto,” she said.

The defeat dealt a major blow to efforts to establish the first comprehensive federal framework for digital-asset markets – and offered another illustration of Congress’s struggle to keep pace with disruptive new technologies as lawmakers wrestle with a similarly fraught debate over artificial intelligence.

Tillis switched his vote from yes to no in a procedural move that preserves his ability to bring the measure back up for reconsideration later.

Community banks fiercely opposed provisions allowing rewards on stablecoin holdings, arguing they could pull deposits out of traditional lenders and reduce funding available for farmers and small businesses.

Several Republican senators also expressed concerns about those provisions, complicating party leaders’ efforts to muster support for the bill.

The deep-pocketed crypto industry spent hundreds of millions of dollars campaigning to advance the bill.

Trump, who has earned more than $1.4bn from his family’s crypto ventures, had urged Congress to pass it. Trump courted cash from the crypto industry on the 2024 campaign trail, calling himself a “crypto president”.

His regulators, particularly the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, will now be positioned to fill the crypto policy void, but efforts to write favourable rules for the digital-asset industry could prove challenging.

Industry experts have said that only Congress can create a lasting regulatory framework. Without legislation, regulations will be vulnerable to a shifting political climate and court challenges, creating lingering hazards for the crypto industry, executives and analysts said.

The Trump administration’s own extensive rollback of dozens of SEC and consumer watchdog policies introduced under former Democratic President Joe Biden has underscored that risk.

Bitcoin, the world’s largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5 percent as the vote appeared set to fail, its biggest daily percentage decline since June. Shares of crypto exchange Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as 10 percent.

articles.title: Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner after intense grassroots campaign
articles.excerpt:
Three-month-old Jabal was returned to Park Slope bodega after community rallied to rescue purloined kitty

The owner of a New York City bodega on Tuesday was reunited with the store’s cat after a coup...
articles.body_text:
Three-month-old Jabal was returned to Park Slope bodega after community rallied to rescue purloined kitty

The owner of a New York City bodega on Tuesday was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort.

The plight of three-month-old Jabal began on Thursday morning in Brooklyn, when he went just outside the Eighth Street Mini Market where he lives as it opened for the day. A man walking alongside a woman passed the Park Slope market then picked up Jabal, and the pair took off as the kitten visibly squirmed, according to store surveillance video which the bodega’s owner, Imad “Jimmy” Innab, reviewed after he noticed the cat had gone missing.

Dan Janzen, who lives across the street from the Eighth Street Mini Market and is one of its regular customers, said someone immediately ran after the couple and told them the kitten belonged to the bodega – but they were unmoved, stuffed Jabal into a bag and left with him anyway.

As the New York Post and the local CBS affiliate soon reported, Innab and his family subsequently offered a $500, no questions asked reward for Jabal’s safe return, which was announced on a poster. Supporters of the bodega also canvassed the streets of Park Slope for Jabal while the neighborhood’s forum on the Reddit platform provided updates on the search efforts.

One thread dedicated to Jabal’s disappearance had a photo of the couple who took the kitten and was titled, “Anyone Know These Two?” It generated about 1,000 upvotes – which indicate Reddit users’ approval of a thread – and more than 240 comments, with many aiming to help reunite Jabal with the Innabs.

Another thread titled “Stolen Bodega Cat?!?” also called attention to Jabal’s catnapping, along with the news media coverage, which publicized the shocking surveillance footage of the kitten being brazenly snatched.

The campaign paid dividends by Monday, when Janzen – speaking on behalf of Innab’s store – said the bodega had received a call from someone claiming to know who had Jabal. That person said Jabal would be brought back to the store from the Brooklyn neighborhood of Bushwick, according to both Janzen and Innab.

Janzen on Tuesday afternoon then followed up with pictures of Innab holding Jabal, including one in which the bodega owner was planting a kiss on the top of the kitten’s head.

Janzen sent the joyous pictures after spending part of Monday and Tuesday at the store with Innab eagerly awaiting Jabal’s return.

“As much as we love the kitten, we love him more,” Janzen said of Innab. “We were rallying around him to keep his hopes up.”

The Post on Tuesday reported that the woman seen leaving with Jabal arranged for her stepson to bring the kitten to the New York police precinct in Park Slope. Police then brought Jabal back to Innab’s bodega.

Furthermore, the Post reported that the police took the woman into custody on Tuesday, but she was not yet booked with a crime. Innab had previously said he only cared about Jabal being returned safely and did not want to see the pursuit of criminal charges in the case.

Innab also spoke about how had been particularly affected by Jabal’s snatching because the Eighth Street Mini Market’s prior bodega cat, Victoria, had died in June after living there for 17 years. Innab took in Jabal to succeed Victoria, and the kitten was soon due to be given a microchip, which is injected subcutaneously and contains scannable owner and home address information.

Bodega cats are deeply embedded in the fabric of New York City, serving to help keep vermin under control while also acting as living mascots for the stores where they reside. They can be seen lounging among store offerings or roaming along the freezer cases – among assorted other activities – in pictures on certain widely followed social media accounts, including @bodegacatsofnewyork on Instagram.

Janzen on Monday made it a point to say that Innab refused to entertain the thought of not getting Jabal back. As Janzen put, Innab “always said, ‘I have a feeling he’s coming back.’”

“I wish all the stories in the world could end this happily,” Janzen said on Tuesday.

Innab said the way the neighborhood where his store had stood for 39 years supported him after Jabal’s temporary abduction “means everything” to him.

“The people are very beautiful – very good – here,” Innab said of Park Slope. “And I thank everybody who tried to help me.”

articles.title: Air pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggests
articles.excerpt:
Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide

Air pollution is associated with an increased risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts,...
articles.body_text:
Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide

Air pollution is associated with an increased risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, according to research.

Environmental pollution is known to be associated with poorer mental health but its role in suicide risk is less well understood. Scientists at Queen’s University Belfast examined whether air, noise, light, and water pollution could influence the risk of death by suicide and suicidal behaviours.

Their meta analysis of 29 studies found that exposure to airborne small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide were linked to a heightened risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.

Narrative analysis of a further 16 studies suggested that some other air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone, as well as noise pollution, were also associated with a higher suicide risk. However, evidence for light and water pollution was inconclusive.

The authors said the findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, suggested that environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies and that suicide prevention should also be viewed as a public health issue.

“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they said.

“Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing.”

But other experts expressed caution about the findings. Dr Jess Moody, the senior research and evidence manager at Samaritans, said: “While the reasons for suicide are complex, evidence shows that a variety of factors can impact suicide risk and we must not ignore the environments we live in, particularly inequalities around living conditions. Samaritans welcomes research that helps awareness of how suicide links to wider public health concerns.”

Dr Jon Van Niekerk, the chair of the general adult faculty at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said the research suggested some forms of air pollution may be associated with a small increase in suicidal behaviour but it did not establish that air pollution itself caused suicidal thoughts or attempts.

He added: “Air pollution is closely associated with other factors which we know can influence mental health, including socioeconomic deprivation, urban living, physical health and housing.

“The study provides further population-level support for reducing harmful air pollution, though the findings should not be seen as supporting individual suicide risk prediction or suggesting that pollution reduction alone could be a suicide prevention measure.”

Dr Rosie Cornish, a senior research fellow in epidemiology and health data science at the University of Bristol, said there were many factors associated with higher levels of air pollution as well as increased risk of suicide.

“If air pollution is not actually a cause of increased risk of suicide then reducing pollution will not help to prevent suicide. The authors do not acknowledge this when drawing their conclusions.”

Dr Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge, said: “This study confuses two fundamentally different concepts: causation and association.

“There are many other factors that could potentially explain the associations observed. For example, areas with higher levels of pollution may differ in other ways that affect suicide risk.

“This research finds factors that are associated with increased suicide risk, but further research is needed to claim that the factors identified are causes of increased risk.”

More than 720,000 people globally die by suicide each year. It is the third leading cause of death among 15– to 29-year-olds, according to the World Health Organization.

articles.title: Pocock says Labor easing copyright protections for AI datacentre investment would throw creatives ‘under the bus’
articles.excerpt:
Proposals revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Albanese ministers

The Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ work...
articles.body_text:
Proposals revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Albanese ministers

The Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as its pursues a compromise with American tech giants.

The proposals were revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Labor ministers and warned Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company training models locally.

The independent senator David Pocock said the compromise would throw protections for creatives and copyright holders “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.

“It would mean putting AI companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content, unless they opt out,” Pocock said on Tuesday.

“The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights they already hold over content they create and own and invest in.”

The proposals were contained in a document Pocock described as screenshots of government’s consultation proposals, tabled in the Senate on Tuesday and titled “AI on Australian Terms”.

AI companies have sought to train their models on content and data online but cannot do so with Australian content due to local copyright rules.

The document raises as a key issue the vast number of small individual creators of online content, for which voluntary deals with AI companies “is not realistic/possible”.

It suggests requiring rights holders “digitally protect” their material if they do not want AI models trained on it – a proposal rightsholders say is not feasible.

Under one option it proposes, AI companies would gain the right to access and train models on any unprotected online material as long as they made deals with enough businesses.

Under another, AI companies would do deals with creatives’ rightsholder organisations that give the access rights even if the content was made by someone who was not a member of the organisation that won the deal. A licence to access one category of material, such as music or text, would be extended to cover the many different small creators within that industry.

Labor’s industry minister, Tim Ayres, had on Monday said the government’s forthcoming AI rules would “in no way” involve a reduction in copyright protection.

The deputy prime minister Richard Marles, said the federal government was “working at a pace” to respond to the issue of copyright, and maintained the opportunity to work with American tech giants was a “significant moment for the country”.

“The opportunity for Australia economically is enormous in collaborating with frontier companies … and having frontier training occur in Australia,” he told the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening.

“We want to see this opportunity come to the country [but] it needs to come on terms which are in our national interests.”

Marles confirmed the federal government had spoken with tech companies in San Francisco in the past fortnight on the issue, adding “I think this can be done”.

The Greens senator Sarah Hanson Young said the suggestions of a copyright compromise were “abhorrent” prior to the revelations on Tuesday afternoon.

“Every Australian deserves to get paid for the work that they make and the work that they do,” Hanson-Young said.

“A weakening of the copyright laws letting big tech take the work of Australians for free, not have to pay for it, for their own profit.”

Musicians, writers and artists lobbied against weaker copyright laws earlier this year after reports AI companies were offering $50bn datacentre investments in exchange.

The attorney-general, Michelle Rowland, is running the government’s ongoing consultation with affected organisations.

A spokesperson for Rowland on Tuesday said the government would ensure any future copyright changes deliver “meaningful control and fair compensation”.

OpenAI’s vice president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, met ministers and officials this week, as the company considers investing in Australia.

In an interview with The Australian newspaper about the prospect of training models here, O’Leary said: “Our company isn’t ready to have that conversation if we can’t get through the gating problem of the copyright barriers.”

The newspaper reported the comments as an “ultimatum” that sought to “strong-arm” the government. Marles said the newspaper was “overstating” the comments. OpenAI has asked the paper to correct its headline and article.

Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told News24 on Tuesday he hadn’t seen any ultimatum and he would reject one if it were issued.

“We want to support Australian artists,” Charlton said. “We want to give them control over their work. We want to make sure they’re compensated, if they choose to have it used.

“We’re not compromising them or trading them off. So if we lose some datacentres over this, so be it.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
articles.excerpt:
At San Francisco conference Dario Amodei reiterates need for AI slowdown as Jensen Huang argued against it

Anthropic’s CEO took to the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate h...
articles.body_text:
At San Francisco conference Dario Amodei reiterates need for AI slowdown as Jensen Huang argued against it

Anthropic’s CEO took to the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call for a slowdown of AI development. Following shortly after, Nvidia’s CEO argued against such deceleration.
 Dario Amodei used an automotive analogy to make his point: when a competing car company has a safety incident like brake failures, it is a moment for all car companies to stop and review their own practices, he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention on Tuesday.

“It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.”

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after, “Run as fast as you can.”

Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies, coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and is “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps.

Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have all recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. His comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public.

Huang, who also made an appearance at Dreamforce on Tuesday, said companies should not slow down AI development. He argued that new regulations aren’t necessary, advising AI companies to simply wait to release products until they know they are safe rather than begging the US government to intervene.

Huang said he envisions a future where “every company, every enterprise … would become an AI company”. He said companies will become more ambitious when armed with AI and reiterated the idea that those who don’t embrace the technology will get left behind.

He also pushed back on the idea that AI is going to destroy jobs, calling it “completely nonsense”.

One day prior at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, Donald Trump called Huang while the CEO was on stage. Huang put the president on speakerphone as Trump called the growing concern about AI a “hoax” and asserted again that a slowdown would only benefit China.

Huang responded: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America.”

The rising concern over AI comes as both OpenAI and Anthropic head for initial public offerings, which could give investors and the public insight into the companies’ finances. Some analysts have predicted the IPOs will be among some of the largest in history. Amid the AI panic, Altman said he plans to delay OpenAI’s IPO until next year over safety concerns.

At Dreamforce on Tuesday, Amodei said the thing that surprises him most about AI is the speed of its proliferation.

“It’s been the pace of the progress – not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he said about the growing adoption of AI. “We had a prediction of just how capable these models would be. But I think what we didn’t appreciate is that it would lead to these companies growing so fast.”

articles.title: Michael Rapaport cheers Macklemore getting dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour, says 'f--- you'

Michael Rapaport shares how much speaking out on Jewish hate following October 7th changed his life

Actor Michael Rapaport celebrated singer Macklemore's removal from Ed Sheeran's tour on Monday afte...
articles.body_text:
Michael Rapaport shares how much speaking out on Jewish hate following October 7th changed his life

Actor Michael Rapaport celebrated singer Macklemore's removal from Ed Sheeran's tour on Monday after Macklemore repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind’s Hall" as his opening act.

"Macklemore don't rap no more, you got kicked off the tour. That's a better verse than anything you've done in your ridiculous career as a non-rapper," Rapaport said in a video on X.

"Anti-Jewish 'rapper' Macklemore was kicked off the tour with Ed Sheeran," he added. "Now you can go back to your home in Washington State that's on stolen land and take up an instrument. Take a dance class. Take a singing class. Learn how to tinkle the piano. Because when people come out to see a musical performer, you need to perform music, not spread bulls--- lies about a fake genocide, a fake occupation and a fake apartheid. F--- you, OK?"

MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE

Michael Rapaport ripped Macklemore after the rapper called for a "Free Palestine" and performed an anti-Israel song while opening for Ed Sheeran last week. (Bobby Bank/Getty Images; Kieran Frost/Redferns)

"You got plenty of time now. I want you and all your 'Free Palestine' p---- a-- motherf---ers to go back and watch some of these videos from Oct. 7. OK, motherf---er? Macklemore, you non-singing, non-dancing bulls--- artist and the rest of you 'Free Palestine' propaganda-pushing motherf---ers. Oh yeah? L'shana Tova!" Rapaport concluded.

Fox News Digital reached out to Macklemore's representation for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rapaport previously attacked Macklemore after the rapper appeared in a video giving a speech defending his use of the stage to push political messaging.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," Macklemore said in a video shared on social media.

PINK HITS BACK AMID BACKLASH FOR CRITICIZING MACKLEMORE'S PRO-PALESTINIAN CONCERT REMARKS

Singer Macklemore faced backlash for a speech he gave during Ed Sheeran's tour defending his political activism. (Arnaud Finistre / AFP via Getty Images)

"I said, ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," he continued.

"Imagine going to see Ed Sheeran & this absolute no-talent non-singer, non-rapping, non-dancing clown, Macklemore, is opening & because he actually has no act or specific skill set, he’s jumping around like dkc carrying on about a genocide that never happened in Gaza," Rapaport wrote, adding, "This is a nightmare."

Rapaport, who is Jewish and has frequently spoken out in defense of Israel, told Craig Carton on his new OutKick program, "The Craig Carton Show" that his pro-Israel stance has been an "issue" for him in 2026.

"No, the — yeah, the career stuff has been a problem," Rapaport said. "There's been an issue. The show's being boycotted. Sucks. It doesn't make anybody comfortable. It doesn't make the club comfortable. It doesn't make the other comedians comfortable."

BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM

Michael Rapaport has said that he has faced backlash for his pro-Israel stance. (Charles Sykes/Bravo via Getty Images)

He added that he has been verbally attacked and threatened for his stance in New York City.

"Anti-semitic, anti-Jewish stuff," Rapaport said. "That hurts me, it embarrasses me, I don't want any other Jewish people behind me to feel uncomfortable, or scared or hesitant to fight, stand up and be proud, however they do it."

However, several prominent figures criticized the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour, including far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

"Absolutely ridiculous position from an ultrazionist trump supporter, who's been awarded by bb for combating israel's critics. its clear that our billionaires are placing their emotional support apartheid state and its genocide over free expression. we must not let this happen," Piker wrote on X Monday.

Outkick Culture's Ian Miller contributed to this report.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

It’s been building for ...
articles.body_text:
"Look, Landry said it tongue in cheek, but there's always a little bit of truth to saying something like that, tongue in cheek. If there were no concerns, it wouldn't be said"

It’s been building for ten months, and Lane Kiffin’s return to Oxford is finally here.

The former Ole Miss head coach will officially return to town Saturday afternoon as LSU’s head coach, and the city is making sure every security measure is in place.

Usually, this would be just another weekend of SEC football in the South. Parties in the 'Grove,' fans enjoying the tailgate scene, bars overflowing into the streets as supporters keep themselves lubricated during the day and the police department only dealing with a smaller number of problems.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

ELLA LANGLEY, DISTRACTIONS AND LANE KIFFIN: PETE GOLDING CALLS OLE MISS-LSU 'HIGH SCHOOL HOMECOMING'

But, this is obviously not just another game-day in Oxford for the police department.

The built-up frustration over the offseason storylines surrounding Lane Kiffin will finally reach a boiling point before Saturday even arrives.

I don't think folks are underselling the amount of vitriol that will be spewed towards the former Ole Miss head coach when lamenting over the stories created over the past ten months.

Head coach Lane Kiffin of the LSU Tigers in action during fall practice at Tiger Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images)

Also, this won't be Kiffin's first time back in Oxford since his departure, as he has visited numerous times, even taking in a few yoga classes in the process.

His daughter, Landry, still attends Ole Miss, though most of her time is spent in Baton Rouge with boyfriend Whit Weeks. He just also happens to be LSU's starting linebacker, which I'm sure leads to some interesting conversations at practice between him and Kiffin.

But, this weekend is all about a return to the city that put Lane back on the map, and they are waiting for him.

This was not a process created by the local town hall during a weekly meeting.

The amount of police, state patrol, federal law enforcement and out-of-state help that will be roaming Oxford this weekend should make for a pretty safe day in terms of fan behavior.

On Tuesday morning, the Mobile, Alabama, police department confirmed they are sending their crowd-control units to Oxford for the weekend.

"The Mobile Police Department’s Mounted Unit will be in Oxford, MS from Thursday, September 17th – Saturday, September 19th working with local law enforcement during the area’s upcoming event," a spokesperson said in a statement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Mardi Gras in Mobile, Ala. (Getty Images)

In addition to the help from Mobile, the City of New Orleans will also be sending its mounted police to the Ole Miss campus this weekend to provide help with crowd control. Also, sources tell OutKick that there will be additional support for the LSU football team, with Louisiana State Patrol sending additional members to Oxford, more than usual for a road game.

You can expect a large amount of security around Lane Kiffin at all times this weekend, while the school will also take measures to not give out where the team is staying on the night before Saturday's showdown.

Look, there is no love lost between LSU and the Rebels.

Lost in the chaos of Lane Kiffin returning is the fact that these two teams have a storied history in the 'Magnolia Bowl', and there is plenty of hatred already instilled between these fans.

But, that doesn’t mean Pete Golding isn’t imploring his fans to use that Southern hospitality at its finest.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"To me, what this place has always been about, why so many people love coming here and respect this place is because of the people who are here and how they make (other fans) feel when they come here. Be there early and be loud," Pete Golding noted.

"But I think at the end of the day, there’s still a respect piece. And this place has always been known to have really, really good people. Let’s not lose that over a game or a person or anything like that."

Head coach Pete Golding of the Ole Miss Rebels looks on in the first half against the Miami Hurricanes during the College Football Playoff Semifinal at the VRBO Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Jan. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

As for Lane Kiffin, he seemed pretty content with the fact he is playing the villain, which actually takes the attention off his football team, and puts the pressure on Ole Miss.

"I guess there’s real safety issues and stuff, so there’s people that have a plan for that," Kiffin mentioned. "I told the players today, ‘Man, you don’t have anything to worry about as far as, like, attention on you all week and everything. There’s going to be so much attention, hatred, everything on me. You just get to go play. Really, the pressure’s on them."

articles.title: 64 House Democrats help Republicans kill Trump impeachment effort
articles.excerpt:
Rep. Al Green is pushing the House again to vote on impeaching President Donald Trump.

Dozens of House Democrats voted to help Republicans quash an effort to impeach President Donald Trump on Tuesday...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Al Green is pushing the House again to vote on impeaching President Donald Trump.

Dozens of House Democrats voted to help Republicans quash an effort to impeach President Donald Trump on Tuesday.

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, forced a vote on impeaching Trump over federal immigration officials' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year. The move fractured House Democrats, whose leaders have largely avoided placing an emphasis on trying to oust the president as they work to take back Congress in the November midterms.

The House voted to table the measure in a 232 to 147 vote, a maneuver to get rid of it while avoiding voting on the impeachment resolution itself.

Eighteen House Democrats voted with Republicans to table the resolution, while 46 voted "present." Nearly 150 voted to move forward with a vote on impeaching Trump.

OUTGOING HOUSE DEMOCRAT AL GREEN FILES ANOTHER IMPEACHMENT RESOLUTION TARGETING PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was among the Democrats who voted "present" on Rep. Al Green's resolution to impeach President Trump. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images; Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Democrats walked a political tightrope with the bill, forced to choose between appeasing their anti-Trump base and appealing to moderate and independent voters by showing them they were focused on tackling Americans' everyday issues like high cost of living rather than political revenge.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and his top deputies voted "present," avoiding taking a stand on the matter while allowing Republicans to more easily scuttle the resolution.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEM REBELS EXPOSE CRACKS IN JEFFRIES’ HOUSE LEADERSHIP

Jeffries said in a statement that impeachment "traditionally requires a comprehensive investigative process, the collection and review of thousands of documents, an exacting scrutiny of the facts, the examination of dozens of key witnesses, congressional hearings, sustained public organizing and the marshaling of the forces of democracy to build a broad national consensus."

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, speaks during a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol on July 23, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber-stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda," senior House Democratic leaders said. "Accordingly, we will again vote 'present' on the motion to table the impeachment resolution as we continue our fight to make life more affordable for everyday Americans, while committing to holding the crooks accountable using every tool available to us beginning on day one."

But Green railed against Jeffries and other Democrats who did not vote to impeach Trump during his own comments to reporters on Monday.

"They will acknowledge that what the president is doing is impeachable, but they would have us wait. Well, the Constitution doesn't have a wait clause in it," Green said. "I believe that there are some Republicans and Democrats who are considering voting to protect the president. If they're not considering protecting him, that will be the effect of what they will do when they vote to either table or they vote to send this to a committee for further investigation."

CONSERVATIVES ERUPT AFTER AL GREEN MELTS DOWN DURING VIRAL CLASH: 'UNHINGED LUNATIC'

Green previously forced a vote to impeach Trump in June 2025, when 128 Democrats joined Republicans in voting to table the Texas progressive's resolution.

It could also be Green's last chance to protest Trump in the halls of Congress — he was among several Democratic incumbents to lose their primary races amid a wider rebellion by left-wing voters against their establishment.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

articles.title: CC Sabathia says Yankees could do a better job helping young players handle the pinstripes: 'Different beast'
articles.excerpt:
Opening Day is tonight, with the New York Yankees facing off with the San Francisco Giants. Colin Cowherd asks if the Yankees are under the most pressure entering this season to win a World Series.

I...
articles.body_text:
Opening Day is tonight, with the New York Yankees facing off with the San Francisco Giants. Colin Cowherd asks if the Yankees are under the most pressure entering this season to win a World Series.

It’s been said many times over a century: earning your pinstripes with the New York Yankees is one of the hardest things to do in baseball.

Just take Anthony Volpe’s rollercoaster career with the ballclub, which has once again become a storyline as they head toward the postseason. Through four seasons, Volpe, a former first-round pick by the Yankees, has been showered with cheers, vitriol and everything in between from the fan base whose expectations will never fall lower than World Series or bust.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

If that’s not hard for a 25-year-old to deal with, Hall of Fame left-hander CC Sabathia was even a bit intimidated by the weight the pinstripes hold when he was a free agent in 2009. He eventually signed on and became a beloved figure in Yankees lore — his No. 52 is set to be retired on Sept. 26 — but he understands it’s not for everybody.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Anthony Volpe of the New York Yankees looks on after the fifth inning against the Colorado Rockies at Yankee Stadium on Sept. 10, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

While speaking at his PitCCh In Foundation’s 6th Annual Golf Classic at Alpine Country Club on Monday, Sabathia suggested to OutKick that the Yankees should come up with a way to not coddle those young players from the expectations, but rather help ease their way into it.

"It’s hard to watch, right?" he said when asked about what Volpe has gone through, especially now that he’s hearing cheers again after performing well following his latest call-up. "Because he’s from here, he wants to do well. And I just watched so many young players for the Yankees, whether it’s Gary Sanchez, whether it was Miguel Andujar, whoever it is, you get a label and that’s what it is, which sucks especially for a young player. I feel like the only young player that came in and did well was [Aaron] Judge because he hit 50 homers and everybody was off his back. So, it’s hard to build up equity with the fan base when you’re so young.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"George Lombard [Jr.] just went through the same thing. He had six errors in a row, and you started hearing grumblings and all these different things. So, it’s hard to develop here as a young player and I think the Yankees need to do a better job to insulating these guys and helping them understand what it is to put on the pinstripes. There’s going to be ups and downs, you gotta cancel out the noise and go out and play baseball every single day."

Of course, it’s easier said than done in a New York market where championships, no matter the sport, are expected each time a season begins. But the only way through is forward for players like Volpe, whose ups and downs since reaching the big leagues have kept fans guessing. They see what could be, but consistency hasn’t been there for the highly touted prospect.

CC Sabathia speaks at his PitCCh In Foundation's 6th Annual Golf Classic on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026 at Alpine Country Club in New Jersey. (Cesar Nunez)

"You think about Volpe’s perseverance and determination — what else is he going to do? He’s not going to quit," Sabathia added. "This is what he wanted to do his whole life. He wanted to play baseball his whole life, and he’s been in tough situations. Baseball is a hard game, but I think he’ll be better for sure, whether he’s playing second base, whether he’s playing shortstop in the Bronx or somewhere else.

"Wherever it is, he’s talented enough to play the game. Hopefully he can do some things well and help us down the stretch. Jazz can get healthy, they can platoon. We’ll see what happens. But I’m super excited for his future, not only here but if it’s somewhere else, too."

Sabathia spent 19 years in the major leagues, where expectation was immediate for him as well coming up with the Cleveland Indians in 2001 as a 20-year-old. He felt that pressure there, and even for the half season he played with the Milwaukee Brewers.

But arriving in New York was a different story in 2009. Sabathia and the rest of his star teammates came through, though, winning the World Series that season and giving a franchise synonymous with titles its 27th to extend the MLB record.

Since then, the Yankees haven’t been able to add their 28th, making just one Fall Classic in 2024 before falling to the Los Angeles Dodgers. Sabathia hopes this could be the year the Yankees get back and see it all the way through so his squad isn’t still the last New York team to win it all.

But then again, the pressure is immense to make that happen. It’s already begun as the Yankees clinch yet another postseason berth and the chance to hoist the trophy at the end of the season.

It’s pressure Sabathia feels is found nowhere else in MLB, especially for young players trying to make a name for themselves on one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world.

Anthony Volpe of the New York Yankees is in action against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium on Sept. 12, 2026. The Mets defeated the Yankees 12-2. (Getty Images)

"This is the only place it happens. If you think about anywhere else, it doesn’t happen anywhere else. You think about what Roman Anthony is going through in Boston. If that was here in New York, it would be leading Sportscenter every single day," Sabathia said.

"It's a different beast when you put on the pinstripes."

articles.title: Romanian shepards and farmers clash with police
articles.excerpt:
Riot police have clashed with Romanian shepherds and farmers as they rioted during a protest against a ban on livestock exports due to disease.

About 2,000 people gathered to demonstrate in the capit...
articles.body_text:
Riot police have clashed with Romanian shepherds and farmers as they rioted during a protest against a ban on livestock exports due to disease.

About 2,000 people gathered to demonstrate in the capital, Bucharest, on Tuesday against the extension of a live sheep export ban, imposed by the European Union due to the highly contagious small ruminant plague. As in other protests by farmers across Europe in recent years, the rally was encouraged and supported by far-right forces.

Violence broke out in front of the Romanian government building in Bucharest when some protesters demanding the reversal of the ban began throwing rocks, metal barriers and other objects at law enforcement.

Police responded with tear gas in a bid to disperse them. Twenty-six people were detained, riot police said in a press release.

Twenty-four demonstrators and police officers required medical attention – some for broken bones, others for the effects of the tear gas. Four were hospitalised.

The government and the opposition called on the demonstrators to refrain from violence.

The demonstration was called by farmers and shepherd groups. Protesters held banners calling on the country’s president and prime minister to resign.

Some chanted the name of far-right politician Calin Georgescu, a former presidential candidate who is standing trial for acts against the constitutional order following the annulment of the presidential elections in 2024.

Supporters of Georgescu had shared messages on social media ahead of the protest, asking people to join.

George Simion, the leader of the main far-right group in the country, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), wrote on Facebook that “AUR stands with the farmers and all working Romanians”, but called on protesters to demonstrate peacefully.

The Romanian government said in a press release that the protest had “degenerated into regrettable acts of violence” and called for “calm”.

President Nicusor Dan condemned the “extremely serious” violence and “any attempt to turn a legitimate protest into street fighting” in a social media post.

Romanian shepherds had protested outside the government building at the end of July over the EU ban on live sheep exports, which expires at the end of 2026.

The country of 19 million people has been struggling for months with the highest inflation in the EU and a political crisis with no end in sight.

The pro-European government, which adopted austerity measures to rein in a high budget deficit, was brought down in a no-confidence motion in May, and a divided parliament has failed to confirm a successor.

articles.title: NFL Week 1 proper reactions: Rams panic, Bears hype and Chargers doubts need patience after one game
articles.excerpt: Colin Cowherd lists his power rankings entering Week 2 of the 2026/27 NFL season, including the Kansas City Chiefs making a reappearance, and the Chicago Bears climbing up the ranks after an impressiv...
articles.body_text:
Colin Cowherd lists his power rankings entering Week 2 of the 2026/27 NFL season, including the Kansas City Chiefs making a reappearance, and the Chicago Bears climbing up the ranks after an impressive Week 1.

The NFL is officially back! All 32 teams have now played exactly one game. Yet, people are going to act like that one out of 17 games is plenty of information to inform us about how the rest of the season will go.

NFL WEEK 1 TAKEAWAYS: BENGALS FLASH CONTENDER UPSIDE, BEARS EXPLODE AND PACKERS COLLAPSE

There's arguably no bigger overreaction week on the entire sports calendar than the week between Week 1 in the NFL and Week 2 in the NFL. After months of practically zero information, we finally saw teams on the field playing games that matter.

But we must remember that Week 1 accounts for 5.9% of the entire season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Fans and media are excited to have the NFL back, which often leads to major overreactions following Week 1. (Getty Images)

People in the sports media are going to arrive at wild conclusions based on that minuscule sample size. What if you hired a home inspector for a house you wanted to buy and the inspector came back and said, "Hey, here's 5.9% of my report on this house and nothing more. You ready to make an offer?"

But here we are, every season, making decisions based on less than 6% of the information. Nonsense. Let's take a look at some of the vast overreactions seen across the landscape and break them down.

Of course, this is a major overreaction. The Rams entered the season as favorites to win the Super Bowl, rightfully so, and it seems like everyone is quickly jumping off the bandwagon. Rich Eisen Show producer and on-air contributor Chris Brockman predicted the Rams’ "dream team" would follow the 2011 Eagles and miss the playoffs.

There are two problems with this overreaction. The first, and most obvious one, is that it was one game against a good divisional opponent in Australia. Honestly, the Rams were way too cocky going into the game and traveling across the globe 28 hours prior to kickoff was a clear miscalculation. The 49ers went to Australia a week in advance to adapt to the weather and time change.

INTRODUCING OUTKICK'S FIRST ORIGINAL ANIMATED SERIES, 'SPORTS TALK WITH CAL MCCALLISTER'

The second is that the Rams weren't really at full strength. Aaron Donald didn't play, and Myles Garrett played through a lingering knee issue and is now out for at least four games. Los Angeles didn't generate much pass rush and didn't sack Brock Purdy a single time. That's not going to continue throughout the season.

Also, sometimes a team can get caught drinking its own Kool-Aid. No team entered the season with more hype, with some calling them a "super team" where a Super Bowl seemed like the only option. If anything, Week 1's disastrous result might have been the best thing that could have happened. The Rams got an early wake-up call and I expect them to bounce back in a big way over the next few games.

The Bears obviously looked great in Week 1, dropping a team-record 59 points in a season opener. Caleb Williams showed off his athleticism and playmaking abilities throughout the afternoon, and Bears fans have reasons to be excited. Bucky Brooks posited that Chicago might average 40 points per game, which would easily set the record for points in a season.

But let's pump the brakes just a tad, shall we? First, the Panthers defense isn't exactly a juggernaut. The team gave up some big numbers last season, including 42 to New England and 40 to Buffalo. In addition, Week 1 scoring was up big across the board. Teams don't play their starters much during the preseason which puts defenses at a big disadvantage. A lot of these guys have barely hit any opponents at full speed since last season and practices have gotten much less physical due to concussion and injury concerns.

Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears put on an offensive show in Week 1 against the Carolina Panthers. (Getty Images)

Chicago also benefited from several positive luck factors. The Panthers turned the ball over three times and committed 11 penalties for 84 yards. The Bears converted all four red zone drives into touchdowns and picked up 10-of-14 third downs. Yes, that's what good offenses do, but that ridiculous efficiency is unsustainable over 17 games.

Then, there was the large number of big plays. Three different Bears (Williams, D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai) all had at least one carry of at least 29 yards and four different pass catchers (Kalif Raymond, Rome Odunze, Luther Burden, and Cole Kmet) had at least one reception that went for 20+ yards. Again, great offenses produce explosive plays, but this was an outlier. The Bears are going to be good, and the offense is going to score points, but we shouldn't set the expectation at 40 points scored per game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Chargers looked terrible in a Week 1 upset loss against the Arizona Cardinals as nine-point home favorites. The Cardinals blocked a punt, intercepted Justin Herbert and held Los Angeles to just 117 yards of offense in the second half. Mike McDaniel’s offense was supposed to unlock even more from Herbert, but it produced only two scoring drives, and one was aided by a 48-yard pass-interference penalty.

That kind of debut makes it tempting to declare the McDaniel-Herbert pairing a failure after one game.

Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel looks on as quarterback Justin Herbert warms up before a preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers. (Getty Images)

To be clear, I'm not declaring that this team is destined for great things, but burying them after Week 1 is also a mistake. McDaniel's offense is unique, and it takes time to get used to, especially for offensive linemen. The Chargers have two stud tackles, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt, but are breaking in an entirely new interior offensive line, including a rookie center. They made a lot of mistakes, but they will improve as the season goes along.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Remember that Tua Tagovailoa thrived under McDaniel for multiple seasons and there's no reason to think that Herbert can't have more success than Tagovailoa. I do have concerns about the team's receiver corps, since the Dolphins had Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, but Ladd McConkey is great and if they can get moderate production from the likes of Tre Harris and Quentin Johnston along with contributions from tight ends David Njoku and Oronde Gadsden, the offense will be fine.

That all being said, the Chargers clearly had too much hype coming into the season. While I don't think they're nearly as bad as they looked against Arizona, this doesn't appear to be a team that will seriously challenge for AFC supremacy, either. The Chargers might have been overhyped, but one bad Sunday doesn’t make McDaniel the wrong coordinator for Herbert.

To close, I'm going to share a few overreactions that might not be overreactions at all:

OK, that's it for Week 1. Remember that we've still got 94% of the season to play, so don't get too excited or too disappointed. Unless you're a Dolphins, Browns or Titans fan, in which case you guys should start thinking about 2027.
