articles.title: Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election
articles.excerpt:
Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share

Polls have opened in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the populist, far-right, ant...
articles.body_text:
Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share

Polls have opened in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is predicted to emerge on top in an election that could have a groundbreaking effect on Germany’s political landscape.

About 1.7 million people are eligible to vote. Polling booths opened at 8am local time and will close at 6pm, when exit polls are expected to deliver an initial indication of whether the AfD has secured enough votes for an absolute majority, enabling it to govern the state.

That would mark the first time the party had won a state government, and the first time since the second world war that a rightwing extremist party had gained power at regional state or parliament level in Germany.

Final polls ahead of the vote showed the AfD to have about 40-41% of support. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.

Currently, the small state is governed by the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, together with two smaller parties. The CDU, on about 23%, under its state prime minister, Sven Schulze, hopes to be able to construct a multiparty coalition to be able to retain power.

The CDU and all other mainstream parties have refused to be in coalition with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.

The AfD’s lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, 35, a photogenic former fragrance salesman with a large following on TikTok who has been celebrated like a pop star.

He has insisted he will only take power if the party receives an absolute majority, and would not tolerate a coalition with another party.

The Saxony-Anhalt election is the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, having failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy and reduce the support for the AfD. Irregular immigration has reduced since he has been in office, but not to the extent that it has appeased the average voter.

If the AfD won convincingly, it would put huge pressure on Merz. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal election in 2029.

If the AfD is elected in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new wind farms.

He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think modern” to “Think German” and to reintroduce the singing of the national anthem in schools.

Siegmund has sought to capitalise on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and to tap into discontent amongst east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens, compared to people from the west.

He turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”.

Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday for a “festival of democracy”.

On Saturday evening, a message beamed onto the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”

The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels to historical developments, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.

The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond, specifically over its immigration policy, which it said would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

The latest poll by the public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday put the AfD on a decisive lead of 41%, with the CDU trailing on 23%, the far-left Die Linke on 11.5%, the Social Democrats on 8.5% and the Greens on 6%. Two smaller parties failed to reach the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament.

Independent election observers are active at polling booths amid speculation from the AfD that voter fraud has taken place, in particular in postal voting, with specific focus on a retirement home. State authorities have denied the claims.

articles.title: US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
articles.excerpt: The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile toward...
articles.body_text:
The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile towards US warships patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz.

Experts have dubbed Iran’s targeting of the two US aircraft carriers a “calculated escalation”, as the months-long fighting is increasingly playing out at sea, with both sides trying to exert control over the strategic strait – a global chokepoint used by Tehran as leverage in the war.

The attacks on tankers come as the US claims that an increasing volume of oil has started to flow through the strait, though the exact figures are still debatable, while the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.

The latest exchanges further dim hopes for a de-escalation through diplomacy as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy supplies and slowed economic growth around the world.

So, what do we know about the latest tanker wars, and where is the conflict headed?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces struck three Iranian vessels, including a tanker off Kharg Island, the hub through which Iran exported 90 percent of its crude before the war.

Another tanker was struck near Jask, and an unladen vessel was hit in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to abandon ship.

CENTCOM said the attacks followed Iranian ballistic missile launches against a US aircraft carrier and navy destroyer, which it said successfully evaded the strikes. No US personnel were injured.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it launched “several ballistic missiles” at the aircraft carrier and destroyer, accusing them of “harassing Iranian ships” and taking part in a naval blockade.

“The Iranians did not only target two ordinary warships – they targeted a missile destroyer and, remarkably, an aircraft carrier … the backbone of the American campaign against Iran,” defence analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera.

“This is a very, very significant development, and it doesn’t come as a surprise that the Americans retaliated.”

Iran then said its forces also targeted three oil tankers travelling through what it called an “unauthorised route” in the Strait of Hormuz and three US-linked vessels elsewhere.

In a statement carried by Iranian broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC navy warned all vessels in the Gulf or near the Strait of Hormuz not to be “deceived” by the US military and to “refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at transiting unauthorised waterways”.

“Otherwise, you will be targeted,” it said.

On Sunday, Iran claimed it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Washington claimed the Iranian tankers it struck were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network financing the IRGC and its regional allies.

Iran has long relied partly on a shadow fleet to circumvent sanctions and sell oil, a source of revenue that has become more important since the US began blockading Iranian ports in April.

Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil supplies flowed, in retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks that began on February 28. Some 20 million barrels of oil flowed daily before the war began.

Hassan Ghashghavi, a lawmaker and spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security Commission, said the attacks on US warships were part of “an existential war with America”, arguing that Washington’s naval blockade “should never have existed” in the first place.

“Naturally, they have acted militarily in violation of all international laws,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that “because America is far from us, it does not see this war as existential”.

Meanwhile, the US has continued to build pressure on Iran to open the key waterway, both militarily and economically.

Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a raft of economic measures to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.

Bessent said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.

This comes despite US assertions of normalcy in the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington insisting the waterway is open and that dozens of ships carrying millions of barrels of oil transit it each day.

Last week, Bessent claimed that some 17 million barrels of crude oil a day had been shipped out recently, according to a report in the United Kingdom’s The Times newspaper. Al Jazeera, however, could not independently verify the claims in the report.

President Donald Trump claimed last month that the US was in “total control” of the strait.

Yet figures from marine analytics firm Kpler show only six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five on Monday, with a 10-day average of just 13 vessels per day.

The attacks are adding to concerns about global energy supplies.

Brent crude futures closed on Friday at $96.28 a barrel, their highest level since July 24, up from roughly $70 before the war.

Predictably, US oil and gas prices have also skyrocketed, coming at a crucial time for Trump as Americans head to the polls for midterm elections in November.

Diesel hit a new record price in the US on Friday, soaring to an average of $5.85 a gallon ($1.55 per litre) for the first time ever. Polls have repeatedly suggested a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has also plunged Trump’s popularity.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted in late August found that only 31 percent of Americans back the war, while 63 percent are against it.

The same polling suggested Trump’s approval rating has dropped to 33 percent, down from 40 percent since the fighting began.

The renewed exchanges of strikes between Iran and the US mark an escalation in the six-month-long conflict, according to the director of the Middle East studies programme at George Washington University, Sina Azodi.

Azodi told Al Jazeera that neither side will “cave in” because it “will not look good on them, so the only option is to escalate”.

He said unless there is a political settlement, the war will continue.

“There’s going to be more clashes between the Iranians and the Americans. There can be miscalculations. There can be more civilian casualties”, especially on the Iranian side, Azodi said.

“The [US] secretary of defence can send more troops to the region, but I don’t think the Iranians are going to back down. They’re going to resist that blockade and impose further costs on the United States.”

He said the goal of the US and Iran is to force the other to back down. “The winner is going to be the one that can accept more costs and punishment,” Azodi said.

Commenting on Iran’s strategy, Ali Akbar Dareini, an analyst at the Center for Strategic Studies in Tehran, echoed Azodi, saying the US attacks on Iranian oil tankers are a “big issue” that Iran cannot afford to let “go unanswered”.

“Does it make Iran surrender? No, it compels Iran. It incentivises Iran to lash out and retaliate” more harshly, Dareini told Al Jazeera.

He said the US naval blockade, coupled with sanctions, is inflicting severe pain on Iran, but added the latter has plans to counter it. Iran cannot tolerate this naval blockade to continue, so Iran is already making preparations to break the siege.

“At the same time, Iran definitely has its own plans to make sure that oil prices will shoot up over $100 per barrel,” Dareini said.

articles.title: Black-clad Dover protesters condemned for ‘dressing up in costumes’ by minister
articles.excerpt:
Business secretary says masked anti-immigration protest was ‘not something we would want’ on British streets

A cabinet minister has condemned the blocking of Dover roads by dozens of masked and black...
articles.body_text:
Business secretary says masked anti-immigration protest was ‘not something we would want’ on British streets

A cabinet minister has condemned the blocking of Dover roads by dozens of masked and black-clad people on Saturday.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said that although peaceful protest was an “essential part of British life”, this differed from “dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives”.

He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “So I would condemn it, but I’d condemn the disruption it caused for local people as well.”

Adding that the situation had been resolved, he said: “Clearly, that’s not something we would want or expect to see on the [streets] of Britain.”

He declined to comment “on the security and policing side of it”, but when pressed on the apparent unpreparedness of the police, he said he thought that “on the whole, the police handled it very well”.

Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by Patriot Platform, an anti-immigration group with links to the far right which styles itself as having a “fierce love for our homeland”.

Kent police attended and engaged with the protest on Saturday, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Protesters had dispersed by lunchtime, and no arrests were made during the incident.

Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 45 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways. Videos shared online showed masked people in black marching on the road in a group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars. The number of people involved was not immediately clear, and police did not give an official estimate. One livestreamer estimated that he was marching with hundreds of people.

Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20, chanting “stop the boats” and “England till I die”.

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, posted on X: “A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by Police. We can and must do better.”

He noted that Kent police appeared to have had “little advance warning”, and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he wrote.

“Concerns around illegal migration are not racist. I’ve said that many times. But what we saw today in Dover is against our laws and not fair on residents.”

In a piece for the Mirror, Tapp suggested that he would like additional officers, including mutual aid from forces such as the Met, mobilised quickly if Dover is targeted again.

He wrote: “The Port of Dover is not just another road junction. It is critical national infrastructure, handling around a third of UK trade in goods with the EU and huge volumes of roll-on, roll-off freight. When Dover stops, Britain feels it.

“And the law matters. Wilfully obstructing a highway can be a criminal offence. New legislation also means police can designate protest areas where concealing your identity with a balaclava or other face covering becomes an offence.”

A government spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.”

articles.title: Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
articles.excerpt: Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun nei...
articles.body_text:
Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood.

The remains were carried on Sunday by family members from Zeitoun to al-Ma’madani cemetery in central Gaza City for burial, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent at the scene, Ghazi al-Aloul.

Civil defence crews and family members had spent weeks digging through the ruins of homes hit during Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Many of the victims were part of the extended Malaka family, which alone lost 55 members.

Al-Aloul said families had waited a long time to be able to bury their loved ones in “known, proper cemeteries”. He said that the chance to bury the remains of family members was “not available to every family”, noting that Israeli forces had destroyed and dug up cemeteries elsewhere in Gaza during the war.

Al-Aloul said the remains, though wrapped in shrouds resembling intact bodies, were often only fragments.

“These are bone remains and remnants of belongings that may have been found on the bodies, especially the children’s,” he said, adding that no complete bodies had been recovered from the site because “the Israeli occupation has prolonged this process, and continues to prolong it and prevent it from being completed quickly”.

Raed al-Dahshan, head of Gaza’s civil defence service, told Al Jazeera his teams had formulated plans to carry out recovery operations for thousands more missing bodies, but said the work was being held back by a shortage of heavy machinery.

“We don’t have equipment, we don’t have protective equipment” for rescue workers, he told Al Jazeera.

Dahshan said the recovery of an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble could be completed in about 90 days with proper equipment, but “if that equipment is barred from entering Gaza … this work will continue for years”.

He said his agency had submitted a detailed list of needed equipment to international institutions and was willing to have that machinery remain under international control rather than with the civil defence directly.

He said crews needed large excavators, personal protective equipment and search equipment to locate remains urgently.

On identifying remains, he said crews rely on survivors and neighbouring families to establish who was in a building and where they were at the time of the strike, supported by a team of engineers who sort and document findings in the field. He said Israeli forces’ failure to warn residents before strikes meant “dozens, even hundreds” of homes still required excavation.

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territories, told Al Jazeera that the scenes were a reminder of “the brutality of this conflict”, noting some of the remains dated back to November 2023.

“Thousands of people are still languishing under this rubble … We’re talking about areas that may be under Israeli military control, 70 percent of Gaza – there’s difficulty accessing these areas to extract these bodies.”

“Accountability must happen … It’s essential that we preserve the evidence we’ve been able to obtain during this sensitive period.”

Gaza’s Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 wounded since October 2023.

Similar recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies of people from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families who were killed in a single strike, as well as more than 500 bodies from the Al-Taj tower site, officials and activists said.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Trump's ballroom win highlights need for serious judicial nominees
articles.excerpt: The Supreme Court has ruled to allow the $400 million White House ballroom construction project to continue in a 5-4 ruling. The decision replaces an order issued earlier in the month that halted cons...
articles.body_text:
The Supreme Court has ruled to allow the $400 million White House ballroom construction project to continue in a 5-4 ruling. The decision replaces an order issued earlier in the month that halted construction in Washington, D.C.

Last year, President Trump ordered construction of a White House ballroom and a secure underground military facility. A DC busybody sued to stop it, and on Aug. 31, the Supreme Court killed this laughable lawsuit by a single vote. Mid-construction, long after the East Wing’s demolition, Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three Democrat women to try to shut down the president of the United States’ security improvement, expressly permitted by federal statute and Article II of the Constitution, to the White House complex. This narrow 5-4 ruling proves precisely why Republicans must continue to nominate and confirm rock-solid constitutionalists all across the federal judiciary.

For decades, the White House hosted large events in outdoor tents, with women’s high heels sinking into the soggy Rose Garden and other White House grounds. But that open setting provides a rich target for terrorists, including too many of today’s Democrats, who wish to harm the president. The threat is all too real. Just over two years ago, Matthew Thomas Crooks nearly assassinated Trump at an open-air campaign rally in Butler, Pa. Two months later, Ryan Routh attempted another assassination of Trump at a Florida golf course. In April, a third would-be assassin attempted to murder Trump in a DC hotel ballroom at the annual White House Correspondents’ Dinner.

The White House helipad and new ballroom extension under construction in Washington, D.C. on Aug. 5, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The dire need for a highly secure White House ballroom is obvious—and presidents and their guests long after Trump will enjoy its beauty, utility, and convenience. The White House regularly hosts heads of state, members of Congress, foreign diplomats, and other high-value targets of America’s enemies. Any reasonable person ought to know that, in these disturbing times, we need the most enhanced security imaginable. Trump acted. He ordered the demolition of the run-down, long-past-its-prime White House East Wing to build a privately funded, 70-foot-tall indoor ballroom, a subterranean military bunker, and rooftop security facility.

WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL

Enter Alison Hoagland, an underworked DC busybody and member of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who claims she leisurely strolls by the White House vicinity about once a month —while real Americans, in real America, work real jobs.

She filed suit, claiming the new ballroom was unsightly and offended her apparently very delicate aesthetic sensibilities. DC U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee who suffers from severe Trump Derangement Syndrome like so many other Republican-appointed DC federal judges, took the bait. He blocked all new above-ground construction for the East Wing unless the subsurface military facility strictly required it.

APPEALS COURT LETS TRUMP RESUME WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION, SEEKS LOWER COURT CLARITY

DC federal judges are legendary for their self-imagined expertise in . . . well, everything. But a judge who has never had a real job in his adult life deluding himself into believing his job is now to moonlight as the construction foreman over the White House complex, instead of the duly-elected president of the United States (who happens to be one of the best builders in the world for over 50 years), is next-level judicial narcissism and lawlessness.

President Donald Trump and Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas, center, and Samuel Alito, right. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Matt McClain/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Unsurprisingly, the Democrat-dominated DC Circuit upheld Leon’s rogue ruling over a superb dissent by U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a former law clerk to America’s all-time-greatest Justice Clarence Thomas. The Trump administration took the fight to the Supreme Court, as these DC federal courts would turn the White House complex into a stop-work construction site for years.

TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT

Article III of the U.S. Constitution requires a plaintiff to have standing. In order to bring suit in federal court, a plaintiff needs a concrete, redressable injury that has already occurred or which imminently looms. Plaintiff/DC busybody Alison Hoagland had nothing but her hurt feelings. The High Court has never held that mere personal offense gives someone the right to bring a federal case.

Five of the six Republican-appointed Supreme Court justices correctly rejected Hoagland’s crackpot standing claim. Ruling for her would let anyone file a lawsuit to stop any government building project in America based on aesthetics and hurt feelings. The majority also torched Leon’s unworkable injunction. Leon, the self-appointed construction foreman as even former U.S. Attorney General William Barr —certainly no Trump cheerleader —mocked him , demanded the White House prove every foot of the project served a critical purpose, a subjective standard that would require endless court appearances, construction delays for years, and unnecessary security risks at the White House complex.

Yet Chief Justice John Roberts ignored this basic logic and decided to pen a truly cringeworthy dissent. He argued standing depends on whether a government building is "iconic." He cherry-picked a century-old quote from Theodore Roosevelt to invent a limitless theory of standing. This ludicrous view came within one vote of prevailing. There must be something in the water in these DC federal courthouses.

A McCrery Architects rendering provided by the White House of the new ballroom. (The White House)

Earlier this year, Leon enjoined lawful sanctions against Francesca Albanese, the International Criminal Court’s head prosecutor. The ICC had issued an absurd arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump rightfully sanctioned the ICC and its officials. But that didn’t faze Leon. Leon protected Albanese simply because her husband and children hold American citizenship. Thankfully, a D.C. Circuit panel stayed Leon’s stunning injunction, and the sanctions against Albanese remain in effect.

TRUMP SUFFERS MAJOR SUPREME COURT DEFEAT AS JUSTICES UPHOLD BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP

Roberts’ record is even worse. He cast the deciding vote to uphold Obamacare in 2012, killed the first Trump administration’s U.S. Census citizenship question in 2020, and protected DACA in 2020. He penned a gratuitous concurrence in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), explicitly noting he was not voting to overturn Roe v. Wade (1973), one of the worst decisions in Supreme Court history.

This June, Roberts delivered his coup de grâce. He authored Trump v. Barbara, an egregiously wrong opinion constitutionalizing birthright citizenship for the children of illegal immigrants–including 1.5 million (and growing) Chinese birth tourists. Roberts' ruling is the gravest betrayal of our most crucial sovereign power as We The People, the sovereign citizens of America: to control who becomes one of us. Yet Roberts’ ballroom dissent read like a fever dream, following a bad bout of Trump Derangement Syndrome.

JUSTICE THOMAS WARNS PROGRESSIVISM IS A THREAT TO AMERICA IN RARE PUBLIC REMARKS

It could have been worse. Bush put former U.S. Circuit Judge J. Michael Luttig on his Supreme Court short list. This is the same Luttig who advocated throwing Trump off the 2024 ballot under the preposterous theory that he committed "insurrection" on Jan. 6, 2021. That ludicrous argument ultimately didn’t garner a single vote at the Supreme Court—not even from the three Democrat women who generally rule against Trump after simply seeing his name in the case caption.

The Article III Project proudly stands with Trump. We demand staunch constitutionalists in the mold of Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito. Decades of spineless Republican judges—particularly in the DC swamp--have severely damaged this nation, and the Article III Project will lead the fight to ensure those days never return. Bold and fearless constitutionalists in the mold of new Trump-appointed U.S. Circuit Judge Emil Bove is our future. We won’t get fooled again.

Michael R. Davis is the founder and president of the Article III Project.

articles.title: Zia Yusuf’s post about Camden council leader is ‘straightforward racism’, says minister
articles.excerpt:

Labour has accused Reform’s Zia Yusuf of “straightforward racism” after...
articles.body_text:
Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee

Labour has accused Reform’s Zia Yusuf of “straightforward racism” after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection was not British.

Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia and the leader of Camden council, has been tipped as an early favourite to contest the London seat for Labour after the former prime minister’s resignation.

Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X last week: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”

The post, which has been viewed 8m times, drew sharp criticism from several senior Reform UK figures during the party’s conference in Birmingham at the weekend. Appearing on Sky News on Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, also condemned Yusuf’s post as “straightforward racism”.

Asked by the presenter, Jon Sopel, for his thoughts on the message, Reynolds said: “Pretty straightforward racism, isn’t it? There’s a potential candidate referenced there; spent decades in this country, huge contribution to her local community, so I think that speaks for itself.”

When Sopel asked whether it was “plain racism”, Reynolds replied: “Absolutely.”

Yusuf has drawn significant criticism for his inflammatory comments on X in recent months, including from top Reform UK figures. Nadine Dorries, the former Conservative minister who defected to Reform UK last year, described the post about Abdi-Wali as “nasty”.

“It was a nasty tweet. Zia Yusuf is a brilliant man, and he’s a genius actually, and he’s an incredible communicator. I wish he closed down his Twitter account,” she told Times Radio.

Laila Cunningham, Reform’s candidate for mayor of London and the daughter of immigrants from Egypt, told the Standard: “I don’t know what he meant by that comment. I read it a few times.

“I didn’t understand what he meant by that comment. Of course, you know, that woman is British. She’s the leader of Camden council. I didn’t understand what he meant by that.”

Reform UK has been contacted for comment.

Abdi-Wali arrived in Camden as a child refugee from Somalia. She has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour.

She was first elected as a councillor in 2022 and became the leader of the council in May, when she said: “Camden has been my home for 35 years. It is the place that gave my family sanctuary, that welcomed us, and that has shaped so much of who I am, what I stand for and what inspired my commitment to public service and to working for the community that welcomed us.”

Labour is expected to announce its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection by Wednesday. It faces a battle against the Green party to retain the seat as Zack Polanski, its leader in England and Wales, is expected to be confirmed as its candidate.

If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

articles.title: House Dems plot Trump investigation blitz if they seize majority
articles.excerpt: House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia spoke to reporters, including Fox News Digital, on his panel’s plans to investigate the Trump administration and Trump family if House Democrats ...
articles.body_text:
House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia spoke to reporters, including Fox News Digital, on his panel’s plans to investigate the Trump administration and Trump family if House Democrats retake the majority.

House Democrats are planning for a slew of investigations targeting President Donald Trump, his Cabinet, and his family if they win the midterm elections.

In just two months, voters across the country will decide which party controls Congress for the second half of President Donald Trump's final term. Historical trends dictate that the party in power in the White House — in this case, Republicans — usually loses one or both chambers.

Democrats in the House of Representatives are already planning for that eventuality, key left-wing leaders told Fox News Digital.

SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS

President Donald Trump pictured in the Oval Office of the White House on Aug. 31, 2026. (Annabelle Gordon/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I'm going to start on the Department of Defense. Our service members are being put at tremendous risk. There is corruption, there's incompetence, there is nepotism at the DoD," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told Fox News Digital.

"There are very disturbing reports about ties between defense money and appropriations programs, and requests by the White House to funnel defense spending to certain companies linked to the Trump family. So we're going to take a hard look at all of that."

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Crow sits on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees, in addition to co-chairing the House Anti-Corruption Caucus. He was also notably one of the impeachment managers who helped lead one of two pushes by Democrats to keep Trump out of power.

Asked if impeachment could pop up again — whether for Trump or his appointees — Crow did not rule it out.

GOP LAWMAKER UNVEILS HISTORIC MOVE TO 'EXPUNGE' BOTH 'MALICIOUSLY FALSE' IMPEACHMENTS AGAINST TRUMP

"It's one of several tools that Congress has to pursue accountability, to get information, and to attack corruption," Crow said. "I won't hesitate to use that tool if that's the right one. But there are other tools available to us, too."

Several impeachment resolutions have been introduced over the last two years targeting both Trump and his officials, but none have gained steam within the wider Democratic Caucus.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., right, joined at center-left by Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., the House minority whip, rallies Democrats against the Republican budget plan on the House steps at the Capitol in Washington on Feb. 25, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)

HOUSE DEMS UNVEIL BILL TO EXAMINE REMOVING TRUMP USING 25TH AMENDMENT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has demurred on multiple occasions when asked about impeachment.

And it likely won't be the first tool in Democrats' arsenal that they'd wield if they win in November, two of their presumptive chairmen suggested. The most likely first approach will be tackling what Democrats see as corruption and mismanagement of federal agencies.

JEFFRIES' REPORTED MEETING WITH KUSHNER ABOUT POSSIBLE TRUMP COOPERATION DRAWS LEFT-WING BACKLASH

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to take over the House Oversight Committee if the chamber flips, told reporters he was already working closely with presumptive House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jamie Raskin, D-Md., on potential investigations.

Garcia told Fox News Digital there were "a few key investigations" he was already looking at.

MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING

"One is going to be the Trump family corruption. The second will be the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Third will be ICE and DHS and the corruption happening there," Garcia said. "We'll also go into anyone that's ripping off the American public from a corporate perspective or CEO perspective. And then lastly, there's a lot of interest in the committee on taking on what's happening to the destruction of our vaccination process and [Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr.]."

Raskin, meanwhile, has already previewed what his panel's investigations would look like. He's sent a flurry of requests for information targeting the business dealings of Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as well as Donald Trump Jr. and FBI Director Kash Patel, among others.

TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS

"The Trump family has turned the entire executive branch into a money-making enterprise, so there’s more than enough corruption and lawlessness to keep Democrats across the House busy for years. Judiciary Democrats are already following the evidence wherever it leads, from the Trump family’s astonishing self-dealing and conflicts of interest to the corporations and law firms that have colluded with this administration for profit, advantage and protection," Raskin told Fox News Digital when asked about his plans.

"We will continue to work together across committees and use every investigative and legislative tool we have to uncover the facts, expose the wrongdoing and its costs for the public, hold the perpetrators and profiteers accountable, and pass legislative cures."

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., speaks during a House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Sept. 17, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)

Republicans have long feared that Democrats winning either the House or Senate will grind the GOP's agenda to a halt in Washington.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., previously told Fox News Digital that he believed Democrats would try to impeach Trump "on Day 1" if they win.

Trump, meanwhile, has maintained his innocence amid an array of accusations from the left.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Karmelo Anthony seeks $250K for murder appeal as questions persist over family’s previous $634K fundraiser
articles.excerpt: Anthony was convicted last week in the fatal stabbing of Frisco teenager Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet and was sentenced to 35 years in prison. The newly released exhibits provide the...
articles.body_text:
Anthony was convicted last week in the fatal stabbing of Frisco teenager Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet and was sentenced to 35 years in prison. The newly released exhibits provide the public with a closer look at the evidence that jurors considered before reaching their verdict.

Karmelo Anthony’s family is seeking another $250,000 to fund his appeal after an earlier campaign raised nearly $634,000 and faced questions over how the money was spent, the family announced at a news conference in Dallas, Texas.

The fundraising push came nearly two weeks after a judge denied Anthony’s request for a new trial. His family and supporters, including attorney Russell Wilson, used the Dallas news conference to outline the appeal.

Anthony, 19, was sentenced to 35 years in prison in June after a jury convicted him of murdering 17-year-old Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet in Frisco, Texas. He has appealed and says he cannot afford to hire an attorney for the appeal.

ANOTHER LAWYER JOINS KARMELO ANTHONY'S APPEAL AS KILLER CLAIMS HE CANNOT PAY FOR COUNSEL

The new fund is intended to cover legal fees, experts and other costs associated with challenging Anthony’s conviction, Wilson said.

Left: Karmelo Anthony is seen in a prison mugshot. Right: Austin Metcalf, who was stabbed to death by Anthony. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice; Jeff Metcalf)

"I think there's a misconception that the motion for new trial denial would have ended an appeal," Wilson said. "It actually is part of an appeal."

KARMELO ANTHONY BLASTS JUDGE IN NEW FILING OVER HANDLING OF MURDER TRIAL

Wilson said the appeal could take more than a year. The trial record is expected to be assembled in October. After that, both sides will make their case in writing, and the Dallas Court of Appeals could hold a hearing.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The request follows a GiveSendGo campaign launched on Anthony’s behalf in April 2025 that raised $633,908 before it was removed from public view following his conviction.

KARMELO ANTHONY CLAIMS HE'S PENNILESS AS BUSINESS RECORDS TIED TO PARENTS DRAW SCRUTINY

Karmelo Anthony's mother, Kayla Hayes, speaks at a press conference in April. (Next Generation Action Network via Facebook)

The earlier campaign was organized by Anthony’s mother and initially set a fundraising goal of nearly $1.4 million. Organizers said donations could be used for legal defense, moving the family, basic living expenses, transportation, counseling and security.

GiveSendGo said the money had been distributed over the previous year for lawful purposes, including legal defense and moving the family, and that the campaign was closed after its stated purpose was completed.

LISTEN: AUSTIN METCALF FAMILY FACING THREATS, FINANCIAL STRAIN AS KARMELO ANTHONY FUNDRAISING DRAWS SCRUTINY

The new campaign page says donations will be deposited into an attorney trust account administered by Wilson and that Anthony’s family will not receive or control the money. The page says the funds will be used only for legal expenses, including filings, transcripts, investigators and experts.

Demonstrators showed support for Karmelo Anthony outside the Collin County Courthouse in McKinney, Texas, on the first day of jury selection in his trial on June 1, 2026. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

The page listed a $250,000 goal and $30,194 raised when viewed by Fox News Digital. Trinicia Ricks is identified as the campaign’s creator, while Wilson is listed as the person who will receive the funds.

KARMELO ANTHONY SUPPORTER REPORTEDLY FIRED AS OTHER BACKERS FACE BACKLASH OVER VERDICT REMARKS

A reporter pressed Dominique Alexander, a civil rights activist who has served as a spokesman for Anthony’s family, about the new request and what happened to money raised through the earlier campaign. The reporter also asked about claims that donations were used to buy a car or house.

"These are deliberate lies," Alexander said. "Why would we ask the question to a family to answer something that clearly was a lie?"

AUSTIN METCALF'S FAMILY HIT WITH DEATH THREATS AS KARMELO ANTHONY SUPPORTERS FACE VIOLENCE ALLEGATIONS

When asked where the previous money went, Alexander declined to explain the family’s fees or say whether any funds remained.

The GiveSendGo page for the Karmelo Anthony Legal Fund lists a $250,000 goal and $30,194 raised. (GiveSendGo)

Alexander said the original fundraiser also helped the family relocate after they faced threats.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"That fund was established to not only help with the legal process, but also be able to relocate this family to safety," he said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Public records reviewed by Fox News Digital previously showed Anthony’s parents, Andrew Anthony III and Kala Hayes, were connected to business entities in Louisiana and Texas. A Texas entity listing Andrew Anthony III as its registered agent became active 24 days after Metcalf’s death.

The records did not show whether either company generated revenue, held assets or received money from the fundraiser. Anthony’s parents have not been accused of wrongdoing.

Anthony has since described himself in court filings as a "penniless, destitute, and indigent person, too poor to employ counsel to represent me on the appeal."

Wilson declined to provide additional details about the defense strategy, saying some issues could become important in future proceedings.

Anthony remains in custody while the appeal moves forward.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Wilson for comment.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Anti-migrant AfD seeks to break Germany’s political ‘firewall’ in historic state election
articles.excerpt:
Nile Gardiner weighs in after European voters appeared to reject far-left progressive policies, leading to significant conservative gains across the continent.

A political earthquake is brewing in Ge...
articles.body_text:
Nile Gardiner weighs in after European voters appeared to reject far-left progressive policies, leading to significant conservative gains across the continent.

A political earthquake is brewing in Germany's east as working-class and young voters appear set to deliver an unprecedented victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

The AfD, which was famously backed by Elon Musk in last year’s national election, has been criticized for being pro-Russia and was accused of being a "right-wing extremist endeavor" by Germany’s domestic intelligence office, has the chance to become the first party outside the mainstream center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) or center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), to win an outright majority in a German state parliament, or Landtag, since World War II.

"The reason Saxony-Anhalt matters," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, who holds a doctorate in political science from Berlin's Humboldt University, told Fox News Digital, "is that the AfD is no longer just knocking on the door of power. It may be close to kicking it open."

TENS OF THOUSANDS OF FAR-LEFT PROTESTERS CLASH WITH POLICE IN ANTI-CONSERVATIVE PARTY RIOTS

Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic candidate with broad appeal in the state, has helped propel the AfD to 43% in state polls, far ahead of other parties. The AfD could possibly win with a majority in the state parliament and form a state government, which would be a first for the party. Saxony-Anhalt will hold elections on Sept. 6. (2026 Getty Images)

Other minor parties have led governing coalitions in German states, but no party outside the SPD or the CDU and the CSU has ever held a single-party governing majority in Germany since the Federal Republic was re-established in 1949.

Janek Treiber, a political science researcher at Dresden University of Technology, told Fox News Digital that if the AfD does win outright in Saxony-Anhalt, their policy influence would be limited due to the German federal system, but warned "you must not underestimate the political symbol this would give. That a single party, and a right-wing party, could rule a German state… The symbol that these parties, that have been ruling Germany since 1949 or the East since 1990, they now lose control. They now lose power. I think this is a much more important symbol than just saying, OK, (the) AfD will change this or that in its local school system or university system."

Schatz described the AfD "a nationalist, anti-immigration party on the far right that has become a powerful vehicle for voter anger at Germany’s political establishment — especially in the former East Germany. It campaigns for much tighter immigration, a stronger emphasis on German national identity, rejection of much of the green agenda and a softer line toward Russia."

An outright win for the AfD, even in Germany’s 6th smallest state, would break through the political establishment’s so-called "Brandmauer," or "firewall." Simply put, other parties refuse to work with the AfD, which is currently the second-largest party in the Bundestag, officially the opposition party, after winning 20.8% of the vote in the February 2025 federal election.

'SEND THEM BACK' CHANTS ROCK EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AFTER LANDSLIDE VOTE TO SPEED UP DEPORTATIONS

The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for the 2026 state election in Saxony-Anhalt (Sebastian Willnow/picture alliance via Getty Images)

In an interview on German broadcaster ZDF, the AfD’s national co-chair, Alice Weidel, advocated for closing Germany’s borders and exiting Europe’s Schengen treaty, saying, "Illegal migration, unchecked open borders, anyone can get in. Our internal security is suffering. People are honestly fed up with this situation."

Weidel added, "All Syrian refugees must have their protected status revoked because the reason for their flight no longer exists. These people must return to their homeland. If they don't leave voluntarily, then they must be deported by force." Adding that many of the 1.3 million Syrians in Germany are being naturalized, "we must stop naturalizing these people who should actually be leaving our country. We have Islamization."

GERMAN OFFICIALS WANT TO KNOW WHY BERLIN ATTACK SUSPECT WAS FREE DESPITE ALLEGED ISIS SUPPORT

Regional elections in the eastern federal state of Saxony-Anhalt will take place on September 6, 2026, and two weeks later, the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the capital Berlin itself will also elect their state assemblies on Sept.20, 2026. (Ronny Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images)

In May 2025, Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" group, citing "anti-migrant positions and an ancestry-based definition of German identity." This past February, according to Deutsche Welle, that classification was put on hold by a German court after "Judges found that while there was evidence of potentially unconstitutional statements and policies within the AfD… it said that there was not sufficient evidence to characterize the party as a whole as extremist."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently told state broadcaster ARD, "I cannot imagine international investors attending a ground-breaking ceremony with an AfD Minister-President to set up new plants and establish new businesses in Saxony-Anhalt… However, that is a decision for ​the voters in Saxony-Anhalt to make. The state will suffer ⁠considerable damage if things turn out as we now fear they ​might."

This has done little to damage the popularity of the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund. In a state of just over 2 million people, he has a TikTok following of over 700,000.

A Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) report said Siegmund’s "polished appearance and professional tone lend respectability, and radical demands blend with footage of a community-oriented politician responding to audience questions… The AfD’s physical presence in the streets and omnipresence in the media helps to push the common populist ‘us versus them’ narrative: The AfD is here for you, the other parties are not."

NEW GERMANY SEX-CRIME FIGURES REIGNITE MIGRATION FIGHT AS EXPLOITATION PROBE EXPANDS

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sparked backlash while remarking about the country's migration policies.  (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)

According to the independent, non-partisan German website Wahlrecht.de, which tracks federal and state election polling, ahead of Sunday’s vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD holds a 41%-23% lead over the CDU, followed by three leftist parties. A party or a coalition needs at least half of the seats to control parliament and name a state Minister-President, essentially a governor. So how can a party with only 43% win an election outright? That comes down to Germany’s unique election system.

"German voters cast two ballots," Schatz says, "One for a local candidate — like voting for your congressman - and one for a party. That second vote, the party vote, is the one that counts. It decides how many seats each party gets in parliament." But there is a caveat: "Any party that falls below 5% gets nothing — zero seats — and those votes are effectively thrown out. Right now, several smaller parties are hovering right at that line. If they miss it, 42% or 43% of the vote can translate into more than half the seats. So Saxony-Anhalt could wake up to an AfD majority government even though a clear majority of voters chose someone else. That would be a first in postwar Germany."

The CSIS report said voters are drawn to the AfD "because, or despite of, its extremist ideology. 60.5% of AfD voters hold a right-wing extremist worldview… At the same time, more than two in five AfD voters think that the party does not sufficiently distance itself from right-wing extremist positions." The report also found that AfD’s "strongest recent gains have been among voters 18–25 years old, where the party tripled its results compared to the 2021 national election."

Treiber said economics is pushing younger voters to the AfD, due to rising expenses and unemployment. He also said that younger voters are "kind of polarized because the other part of the youth in Germany is voting for the left party (Die Linke)."

Saxony-Anhalt may just be the beginning for the anti-establishment parties. Voters in neighboring Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel grew up and began her political career, go to the polls in two weeks. Polling data from Wahlrecht.de shows the AfD leading the ruling SPD 35%-32% there.

Conversely, in Berlin, where voters in the capital also go to the polls in two weeks, the average of recent polling has the far-left Die Linke in a dead heat with the CDU at 20%, followed by the AfD at 18%, with the Greens and the SPD each around 15%. While the majority of the AfD’s support does come from the former East Germany, the party is represented in 14 of Germany’s 16 state legislatures and holds 15 of Germany’s 96 seats in the European Parliament.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

articles.title: Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda
articles.excerpt:
Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades.

The sandwich shop had struggled to mai...
articles.body_text:
Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades.

The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium.

But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced.

articles.title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Bur...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.

During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.

He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.

The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.

“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”

Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.

“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”

His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”

He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.

Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

articles.title: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests
articles.excerpt:
Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession

The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of ni...
articles.body_text:
Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession

The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.

The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.

The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.

The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.

“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”

Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”

Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.

At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.

Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.

Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.

The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”

Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”

Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.

“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

articles.title: Brisbane expected to swelter under hottest September day in years as east coast faces unseasonably warm weather
articles.excerpt:
Queensland capital forecast to hit 34C with local fire bans issued for Ipswich and Lockyer Valley, while Sydney sees reprieve from record heat

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podc...
articles.body_text:
Queensland capital forecast to hit 34C with local fire bans issued for Ipswich and Lockyer Valley, while Sydney sees reprieve from record heat

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Early spring fire bans have been put in place as Australia’s eastern states reckon with unseasonably hot conditions for the start of the season.

The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) warned of unseasonal heat in the low to mid-30s in north-eastern New South Wales and south-east Queensland.

Brisbane had a forecast top of 34C, while Sydney had some respite from the recent record temperatures, with a forecast top of 23C, as that heat moved north.

If Brisbane reaches its predicted temperature peak, it would be the hottest September day in the city since 2019. Brisbane recorded a temperature of 31.6C in the late morning, the weather bureau said, while the Ipswich suburb of Amberley recorded a peak of 35.7C in the early afternoon.

“It’s a bit of an ‘all eyes on the temperatures this afternoon’ type [of] thing until that south-easterly change gets in, which is probably about 6 or 7pm tonight,” the BoM’s Steve Hadley said.

The Queensland fire department issued local fire bans for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley as the state came close to shattering records for the highest temperatures seen in early September.

Areas from Gladstone to the Gold Coast were likely to come a few degrees shy of breaking the record for the state’s highest recorded temperatures for the start of spring.

The state had experienced its third-warmest winter on record with temperatures 1.8C above the long-term average.

BoM meteorologist Jonathan How said over the past 24 hours, a cold front swept across south-eastern Australia, bringing damaging winds, rain and storms.

“At the same time, parts of eastern NSW saw their warmest early spring day on record,” he said.

But a dry cool change was moving up the east coast, bringing milder temperatures from Monday. Western Australia is set to get more rain this week, while Tasmania and Victoria can expect some showers.

South-east Queensland’s fire bans came a day after a similar ban was issued for the greater Sydney region, with early spring temperatures climbing to 33C on Saturday in the NSW capital.

Maximum temperatures across the city during the first days of September matched the midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since observations began.

Severe weather warnings were in place for south-eastern Australia over the weekend as damaging winds fuelled the hot conditions.

Jumping castles were picked up by strong winds in two separate incidents in NSW and Victoria on Saturday.

Two children were treated for head injuries at a scene in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, before being transported to hospital.

An infant with minor injuries was also hospitalised, while a woman was treated at the scene.

Two children in Mount Duneed, near Geelong in Victoria’s south-west, were hospitalised after the jumping castle they were using was lifted into the air.

Temperatures are expected to drop in the coming days across both NSW and Queensland.

articles.title: Volcano eruption triggers flight suspensions at Indonesia's main airport
articles.excerpt:
A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.

Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mou...
articles.body_text:
A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.

Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mount Anak Krakatoa was detected in airspace near Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Sunday morning.

The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said.

More than 22,000 people have been impacted by the suspension of flights, which has been extended until 13:30 (0630 GMT).

The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.

Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.

The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.

Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.

Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity.
